name: fastapprox
baseline: libm expf/logf/powf (single-precision libm; the repo's tests use them as the accuracy reference, libm is never timed)
workload: Test programs (fastapprox/tests/testfastexp.c, testfastlog.c, testfastsigmoid.c, testfastpow.c, ...) assert average relative error over 100000 random inputs against expf, logf, powf, sinf, tanhf, erff and similar, and print million calls per second of the approximation only (1e8 calls on a volatile constant input 1.0f); no libm timing row exists.
claimed_speedup: No speed ratio against libm is stated anywhere in the repo (README is a function list plus one sentence; no results file is committed). Accuracy bounds asserted by the tests against expf/logf/powf: average relative error below 1e-4 for the 'fast' variants (fastexp, fastlog, fastpow, fastsigmoid) and below 2e-2 for the 'faster' variants (fasterexp, fasterlog, fasterpow, fastersigmoid).
stars_or_usage: 13 stars on pmineiro/fastapprox; 222 stars on the romeric/fastapprox mirror and 57 on etheory/fastapprox; the Rust port (crate 'fastapprox' by loony-bean) has 94,746 downloads on crates.io
tradeoffs: Single precision only, two accuracy tiers (fast: about 1e-4 average relative error; faster: about 2e-2). Header-only and usable from C and C++ (one big header, fastonebigheader.h) with SSE2 four-wide v4sf variants of each function. Uses union type punning on the float bit pattern. fastexp clamps its argument at -126 so underflow gives a small positive value; the ChangeLog says that guard cost 25% speed. fastlog has no guard for zero, negative, NaN or infinite input (source read). Also covers lgamma, digamma, trig, hyperbolic, erf, inverse erf and Lambert W.
caveats: The seed lead said the README and tests give speed versus libm; they do not. The README is four lines, the timing macro in tests/testmacros.h times only the approximation function on a volatile constant (1.0f, so a perfectly predictable input), and libm is never timed, so there is no speedup number to quote. The author's original blog post (machinedlearnings.com) could not be reached from this environment (host not resolvable), so any speed claim made there is unverified. Independent hints are indirect: the unrelated SIMD-math-prims README (github.com/mipac/SIMD-math-prims, a different library, CPU unstated) reports expapprox 2366.8M/s against expf 111.3M/s and logapprox 4112.9M/s against logf 115.2M/s, and a search snippet (page not openable) of a BEAST mailing-list thread says glibc exp2/log2 can beat hand-rolled approximations on modern AMD64, so speed against current glibc is hardware-dependent. The repo page shows no detected licence; the BSD-3-Clause terms come from fastapprox/COPYING and the file headers. The page marks pmineiro/fastapprox as a fork of etheory/fastapprox, which in turn is a fork of romeric/fastapprox (222 stars); the code originated in the author's Google Code project. Last commit is the 2017-03-01 merge of an MSVC and gcc narrowing patch.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/pmineiro/fastapprox (README, src/ and tests/ files read; also https://github.com/romeric/fastapprox, https://github.com/etheory/fastapprox and https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/fastapprox for usage)

name: yy_itoa (itoa_yy.c in ibireme/c_numconv_benchmark)
baseline: fmt::format_to(buf, FMT_COMPILE("{}"), val) from fmtlib (the baseline the repo's own itoa report uses); the repo does not time std::to_chars, fmt::format_int or sprintf
workload: Integer to decimal string for u32, u64, i32 and i64 into a caller buffer: 10000 samples per measurement, minimum of 32 repeats, reported as average CPU cycles per call; 'random length' mixes digit counts uniformly (1-10 digits for 32-bit, 1-20 for u64, 1-19 for i64), plus fixed-length sweeps over every digit count; a no-op 'null' group measures loop overhead.
claimed_speedup: Random-length itoa, average CPU cycles per call, GCC 13.2.0 on Intel i5-13600KF: yy 20.69 vs fmtlib 40.37 for u32 (1.95x, derived from page data), 33.55 vs 56.88 for u64 (1.70x), 21.33 vs 53.62 for i32 (2.51x), 33.47 vs 65.65 for i64 (1.96x). Same direction on Clang 18.1.3 (u64 34.10 vs 53.93), MSVC 1940 (u64 42.50 vs 71.73) and Apple M1 Pro with Apple Clang 15.0.0 (u64 26.88 vs 43.44); the null no-op group is about 4 cycles.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2.0 (other reports: Clang 18.1.3, MSVC 1940, Apple Clang 15.0.0); CMake Release build (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE defaults to Release in CMakeLists.txt), GCC gets -falign-functions=64 and Clang -align-all-functions=7; the ARCH_NATIVE option defaults to OFF and the report does not say whether it was used
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i5-13600KF, 5090 MHz reported, Linux 64-bit (GCC and Clang) and Windows 64-bit (MSVC); Apple M1 Pro 3228 MHz, macOS 14.4.1
stars_or_usage: 75 stars on c_numconv_benchmark; the README says the yy functions are used in the yyjson library
tradeoffs: Portable ANSI C with one 200-byte two-digit lookup table and branches on value magnitude; no SIMD and no 128-bit integers. Output is not NUL-terminated and the caller buffer must hold 10 (u32), 11 (i32) or 20 (u64, i64) bytes; the function returns a pointer to the end. The same report also lists a yy_largelut variant that is faster still (u64 random 22.02 cycles on GCC), which per its source header uses 50 KB of lookup tables (the author notes large LUTs are unacceptable in many cases) and is a separate function from the 200-byte-table yy.
caveats: (1) The repo times fmt's compile-time format_to path (vendor/fmt pinned at commit 0379bf3, version not checked), not std::to_chars, fmt::format_int or sprintf; sprintf is registered only as the correctness oracle. (2) The benchmark and the yy function have the same author, but the code, compiler versions and CPU model are public. (3) Cycle counts include loop overhead (null group about 4 cycles); the reported CPU frequency suggests turbo boost was on although the README advises turning it off. (4) The interactive reports are served from github.io, which is not reachable here, so the numbers were read from the report HTML committed under docs/reports. (5) yy is not the fastest in the report: yy_largelut, an and jeaiii beat it in several columns (u64 random on GCC: yy_largelut 22.02, an 29.40, jeaiii 33.32, yy 33.55 cycles). (6) Independent corroboration against the listed baselines, from the raw google/benchmark rows of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/simditoa/benchmarks/HEAD/RESULTS.md (repo https://github.com/simditoa/benchmarks, 0 stars, written by a rival integer-formatting project; Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C c3-standard-8 VM, CMake Release with -mavx512* flags, Ubuntu 22.04 image per its terraform file, compiler version and C++ standard library not printed): geometric mean of ints/s over {UNIFORM_POS, LOG_HEAVY, FIXED 12, 16, 19} is 136.3M for itoa_i64_yy, 62.5M for std::to_chars (2.18x, derived from page data) and 83.4M for fmt::format_int (1.63x, derived from page data). yy beats std::to_chars in every measured shape (1.26x at 4 digits up to 2.97x on uniform 64-bit values) but loses to fmt::format_int on short numbers (1 digit: 525.3M vs 985.8M ints/s; 4 digits: 402.5M vs 454.3M). That file's LLM-written summary scoreboard lists yy_itoa at 103M against std_to_chars 105M, which contradicts its own raw rows (it also gives FIXED:12 simditoa as 295.68M against 189.77M raw), so only the raw rows were used. Because of the unstated compiler that corroboration is tier C by itself.
